summary: Autoscaler thrash in dedicated pool caused by noisy-neighbor IO tail latencies
description:
Issue summary: Several ParcelFlow services using a dedicated GPU pool in us-west experienced repeated P99 latency spikes and transient 429/attach-failures starting 2026-03-13 11:20 UTC. The autoscaler initiated multiple rapid scale-ups and subsequent scale-downs (thrash) which led to perceived GPU shortages for customer routes and elevated token costs.

Impact: Customer Production traffic saw p50->p99 latency widening from 120ms -> 2.4s on batched routes; a small percentage (~3%) of requests returned 429s during attach failures. Throughput for the dedicated pool dropped ~30% during the thrash window. Customer reported increased error rates and degraded user experience.

Environment: Dedicated pool d-ed-usw-7 (prod-us-west / us-west-2). Affected routes are batched-generation endpoints pinned to gpt-j-6b and local-rewrite-v2. Autoscaler policy: predictive+reactive hybrid with cooldown 90s, max GPUs 24.

Timeline (observed):
- 11:18 UTC: background snapshot job from tenant TF-88 begins heavy NVMe upload to long-term storage (sidecar storage-proxy).
- 11:20 UTC: storage-proxy IO tail latency increases (NVMe write lat spikes to 400-800ms).
- 11:22 UTC: allocator observes attach latency increase and begins speculative adds; autoscaler scales up 6 GPUs over 4 minutes.
- 11:27 UTC: p99 latency spikes to 2.4s, several attach attempts time out; autoscaler cooldown expires and aggressively scales down when observed queue drains, releasing GPUs.
- 11:30-11:45 UTC: repeating cycle of attach latency -> scale up -> transient drain -> scale down (thrash) ~4 cycles.

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1) In a dedicated pool, launch a background job that uploads many small checkpoint files through storage-proxy to external NVMe-backed archive while maintaining steady small-batch inference load (1-2 rps per stream).
2) Observe storage-proxy IO tail latencies and allocator attach times.
3) Watch autoscaler decision graph and GPU attach/release events.

Logs and metrics (key links):
- Throughput dashboard: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/throughput?pool=d-ed-usw-7
- Autoscaler event log: https://console.redwood.ai/logs/autoscaler?run=2026-03-13
- Storage-proxy NVMe latency graph: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/storage?host=sp-usw-13
- Kernel/driver alerts: linked in investigation notes below.

Observed behaviour:
- High tail IO latency in storage-proxy correlated 1:1 with attach latency spikes.
- Allocator considered GPUs "attached" slower (nvme stall increased attach handshake).
- Autoscaler interpreted rising attach latency and queued requests as capacity pressure, chose to add GPUs; after short drain, it interpreted low utilization and removed GPUs.
- Resulting oscillation produced short periods where there were not enough warmed GPUs (cold starts) and short periods of overprovisioning while background IO recovered.

Customer-facing note prepared: "We have identified an autoscaler feedback loop tied to high storage IO tail latencies from a background checkpointing process. We're investigating mitigations and a short-term workaround to reduce impact."
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Start a steady inference stream pinned to the dedicated pool. 2) Simultaneously trigger frequent small-file uploads through the pool's storage sidecar (simulate checkpoint churn). 3) Observe storage-proxy NVMe write latency and allocator attach times; verify autoscaler scale events and resulting throughput/latency oscillation.
logs_and_metrics:
Sample logs: allocator/attach: WARN attach_timeout 2026-03-13T11:22:14Z pool=d-ed-usw-7 host=worker-23; storage-proxy: WARN nvme_write_ms p99=712 host=sp-usw-13; autoscaler: INFO scale_up request_id=rl-33 delta_gpus=4 reason='attach_latency_threshold'
Metric snapshots (peak): pool_utilization=78%, p99_latency=2.4s, attach_median=95ms, attach_p99=1.1s.
investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: noisy-neighbor (background checkpoint uploader) caused NVMe write tail which increased storage-proxy latencies. The allocator's attach handshakes rely on low IO latency; prolonged attach times bubbled into autoscaler signals. Autoscaler tuning (short cooldown, aggressive reactive policy) amplified the oscillation.
Actions taken so far:
- Identified offending tenant job using sidecar audit logs (tenant TF-88).
- Temporarily limited TF-88 sidecar upload concurrency via emergency config on sp-usw-13 (reduced tail latencies).
- Increased autoscaler cooldown from 90s -> 180s as a temporary mitigation for d-ed-usw-7.
- Added alloc attach timeout increase to tolerate transient IO blips (short-term).
Next steps:
- Schedule follow-up to evaluate persistent autoscaler policy changes (rate-limits, hysteresis) and improve attach handshake resiliency.
- Work with infra to add QoS to storage-proxy NVMe path to protect inference attach operations from checkpoint upload tail latencies.
- Postmortem to capture long-term mitigations and customer communication plan.
comments: 2026-03-13 11:40 UTC - Marco Rivera (SRE): Scaled down rapid fluctuations by increasing autoscaler cooldown to 180s; observed one fewer oscillation cycle immediately.
2026-03-13 12:05 UTC - Aisha Patel (Support): ParcelFlow notify: they saw ~3% 429s and user complaints of slow responses around 11:20-11:35 UTC. Customer wants ETA for full fix.
2026-03-13 12:30 UTC - Dmitri Ivanov (Infra): Identified tenant TF-88 as source of checkpoint churn; applied concurrency cap on sp-usw-13. NVMe p99 dropped from ~700ms to ~120ms after cap.
2026-03-13 12:45 UTC - Marco Rivera (SRE): Applied short-term alloc attach timeout bump. Monitoring for any regressions.
2026-03-14 09:10 UTC - Lena Chen (CS): Sent interim update to ParcelFlow describing mitigations and next steps; customer accepted temporary workaround and asked for long-term timetable.
resolution_notes: Workarounds applied: capped background upload concurrency for offending tenant and increased autoscaler cooldown; attach timeout slightly raised. These reduced oscillation frequency and recovered throughput to ~95% of baseline. Long-term fixes pending: storage-proxy NVMe QoS, autoscaler hysteresis tuning, and attach handshake backoff improvements. Postmortem scheduled for 2026-03-18.
next_steps: 1) Infra to prototype NVMe QoS on sp-usw-13 and partner hosts (owner: Dmitri Ivanov). 2) Autoscaler team to run controlled experiments on hysteresis and cooldown windows (owner: Marco Rivera). 3) CS to coordinate customer timeline and confirm expected behavior (owner: Lena Chen).
